retrieval.query: What can Harbor customers do today with export scheduling, what are its current limits, and what improvements are planned?

source_chunks.heading: Harbor export scheduling
source_chunks.content:
Harbor workspace administrators can schedule a recurring CSV export of completed orders from the reporting page. The scheduler is available to all paid workspaces as of the September release. Each schedule sends a download link to the administrator who created it; the link expires after seven days. Scheduling does not grant access to other reports, and the recipient still needs an active workspace account to download the file.

The team considers a schedule active once its first delivery has been queued. Workspace owners can pause or delete a schedule from the same page. Pausing keeps the configuration, while deleting it removes the configuration and its delivery history from the page.
source_chunks.uncertainty: Source text has not been reviewed.

source_chunks.heading: Operational limits
source_chunks.content:
A workspace may maintain up to five active export schedules. A schedule runs at most once per day, using the workspace time zone. The current CSV contains completed orders only; pending and cancelled orders are excluded.

The delivery service retries a failed send twice over the following hour. A workspace administrator can check the most recent delivery result in the reporting page, but individual download events are not currently shown there.
source_chunks.uncertainty: Source text has not been reviewed.

source_chunks.heading: Reporting work planned
source_chunks.content:
The reporting group has approved work to add weekly and monthly cadence choices and to include cancelled orders as an optional export filter. Both items are planned for the next reporting cycle; neither has shipped. The group has also recorded a request for an API to create schedules, but no decision or target date exists for that request.

The roadmap is a planning record and does not change the functionality described in the current administrator guide.

retrieval.query: How does Orchard handle a supplier invoice from receipt through approval and payment, and who owns each stage?

source_chunks.heading: Supplier invoice intake
source_chunks.content:
At Orchard, the accounts payable coordinator receives supplier invoices in the shared invoice mailbox. The coordinator checks that each invoice names a supplier and purchase order, then enters it in the ledger with status Received. Missing purchase order details are returned to the supplier for correction; the invoice does not enter the approval queue until corrected.

For invoices with complete intake details, the coordinator attaches the original invoice to the ledger record and routes the record to the budget owner named on the purchase order.
source_chunks.uncertainty: Source text has not been reviewed.

source_chunks.heading: Budget approval
source_chunks.content:
The budget owner compares the invoice amount with the purchase order and confirms that the goods or services were received. If both checks pass, the owner marks the invoice Approved in the ledger. A mismatch is sent back to accounts payable for investigation, rather than being approved automatically.

Approval is the budget owner's decision. Accounts payable maintains the record and communicates with the supplier during an investigation, but does not substitute its own approval for the owner's decision.
source_chunks.uncertainty: Source text has not been reviewed.

source_chunks.heading: Payment run
source_chunks.content:
The treasury specialist includes approved invoices in the next Thursday payment run, provided the due date falls within the next fourteen days. Treasury sends the payment and records the payment reference in the ledger. An approved invoice outside that window stays approved until a later eligible run.

A weekly reconciliation checks payment references against the bank statement. The treasury specialist resolves discrepancies with accounts payable.
source_chunks.uncertainty: Source text has not been reviewed.

retrieval.query: What are the eligibility rules and process for Lumen’s customer credit, and how is the credit applied and tracked?

source_chunks.heading: Service credit eligibility
source_chunks.content:
Lumen offers a service credit when a paid customer's production workspace is unavailable for more than four consecutive hours because of a Lumen service incident. Planned maintenance announced at least 48 hours ahead and outages caused solely by the customer's configuration are excluded. The credit equals ten percent of that workspace's monthly subscription charge.

The rule applies to the affected workspace, not every workspace owned by the customer. A customer must request a credit within thirty days of the incident ending.
source_chunks.uncertainty: Source text has not been reviewed.

source_chunks.heading: Credit request handling
source_chunks.content:
A customer submits a credit request through the support portal, including the affected workspace and incident date. Support verifies the incident window against the incident record and checks the request date. If eligible, support approves the request and forwards it to billing; if ineligible, support explains the reason in the portal.

The portal records the outcome and a link to the incident record so the support team can follow the decision later.
source_chunks.uncertainty: Source text has not been reviewed.

source_chunks.heading: Applying an approved credit
source_chunks.content:
Billing applies an approved service credit to the affected workspace's next subscription invoice. The credit reduces that invoice's amount due and is not paid out as cash. Billing records the amount and support request identifier on the invoice adjustment.

If the next invoice is smaller than the credit, the unused balance carries forward to the following subscription invoice for the same workspace.
source_chunks.uncertainty: Source text has not been reviewed.

Lumen offers a service credit when a paid customer's production workspace is unavailable for more than four consecutive hours because of a Lumen service incident. Planned maintenance announced at least 48 hours ahead and outages caused solely by the customer's configuration are excluded. The credit equals ten percent of that workspace's monthly subscription charge.

The rule applies to the affected workspace, not every workspace owned by the customer. A customer must request a credit within thirty days of the incident ending.
source_chunks.uncertainty: Source text has not been reviewed.

source_chunks.heading: Credit request handling
source_chunks.content:
A customer submits a credit request through the support portal, including the affected workspace and incident date. Support verifies the incident window against the incident record and checks the request date. If eligible, support approves the request and forwards it to billing; if ineligible, support explains the reason in the portal.

The portal records the outcome and a link to the incident record so the support team can follow the decision later.
source_chunks.uncertainty: Source text has not been reviewed.

source_chunks.heading: Applying an approved credit
source_chunks.content:
Billing applies an approved service credit to the affected workspace's next subscription invoice. The credit reduces that invoice's amount due and is not paid out as cash. Billing records the amount and support request identifier on the invoice adjustment.

If the next invoice is smaller than the credit, the unused balance carries forward to the following subscription invoice for the same workspace.

retrieval.query: What is Maple’s enterprise customer retention rate last quarter, and what else is known about enterprise renewals?

source_chunks.heading: Quarter-end snapshot
source_chunks.content:
The commercial operations snapshot reports contract outcomes, not a customer-level retention rate. It does not state the number of distinct enterprise customers represented by the twelve expiring contracts or the number of those customers retained. It also does not provide an approved definition for customer retention.

The snapshot was prepared after the quarter closed and includes open negotiations as unresolved rather than automatically treating them as lost.
source_chunks.uncertainty: Source text has not been reviewed.

source_chunks.heading: Renewal process
source_chunks.content:
An account manager contacts each enterprise customer before contract expiry and documents the customer's decision in the renewal tracker. The finance team validates the commercial terms before a renewal is marked complete. Negotiations can continue beyond the nominal expiry date if both parties agree.

A renewal record includes the contract identifier and its outcome. The process note does not define a customer retention metric or how customers with multiple contracts should be counted.
source_chunks.uncertainty: Source text has not been reviewed.

source_chunks.heading: Enterprise renewal pipeline
source_chunks.content:
At the start of the quarter Maple had twelve enterprise contracts scheduled to expire during the quarter. By the close of the quarter, the account team had recorded eight of those contracts as renewed and two as not renewed. The remaining two were still being negotiated and had not been assigned a final outcome.

The count refers to contracts rather than individual customer organizations. A customer can have more than one enterprise contract.

retrieval.query: How did Quartz’s average onboarding time change from the first period to the second, in days and percentage, and what do the figures measure?

source_chunks.heading: First measurement period
source_chunks.content:
Quartz measured onboarding time for customers who completed onboarding in the first period. The average was 20 calendar days from signed agreement to completed setup. The cohort contained 40 completed onboardings.

The measurement records elapsed calendar time, including weekends, rather than staff hours. Customers who had not completed onboarding by the end of the period were not included in this completed cohort.
source_chunks.uncertainty: Source text has not been reviewed.

source_chunks.heading: Second measurement period
source_chunks.content:
For customers who completed onboarding in the second period, Quartz recorded an average of 15 calendar days from signed agreement to completed setup. This cohort contained 50 completed onboardings.

The operations team used the same start and end events as in the first period and included weekends. This is a descriptive comparison of completed cohorts, not a controlled experiment.
source_chunks.uncertainty: Source text has not been reviewed.

source_chunks.heading: Measurement context
source_chunks.content:
The onboarding dashboard reports elapsed time for completed setups. It does not count the number of hours employees actively worked on a setup. A lower average means completed customers moved from agreement to setup in fewer calendar days on average.

The dashboard does not establish why the average changed between periods; the customer mix and operating conditions may differ.

Quartz measured onboarding time for customers who completed onboarding in the first period. The average was 20 calendar days from signed agreement to completed setup. The cohort contained 40 completed onboardings.

The measurement records elapsed calendar time, including weekends, rather than staff hours. Customers who had not completed onboarding by the end of the period were not included in this completed cohort.

For customers who completed onboarding in the second period, Quartz recorded an average of 15 calendar days from signed agreement to completed setup. This cohort contained 50 completed onboardings.

The operations team used the same start and end events as in the first period and included weekends. This is a descriptive comparison of completed cohorts, not a controlled experiment.

The onboarding dashboard reports elapsed time for completed setups. It does not count the number of hours employees actively worked on a setup. A lower average means completed customers moved from agreement to setup in fewer calendar days on average.

The dashboard does not establish why the average changed between periods; the customer mix and operating conditions may differ.
